Bradley B Fitzgerald Deputy Director

To: Senator Joseph Rafferty Representative Kelly Noonan Murphy Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
From: Christopher Lavoie, Director of Penobscot Regional Communications Center
Re: Testimony in opposition of LD 168, An Act to Improve Safety in Public Schools by Requiring Silent Electronic Notification Systems in Classrooms
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. My name is Christopher Lavoie. I am the Director of the Penobscot Regional Communications Center (PRCC). Due to the wording of this bill, I am writing in opposition to LD 168, commonly known as "Alyssa's Law," in other states across the nation.
Penobscot RCC is Maine's largest Public Safety Answering Point, handling over 65,000 E9-1-1 calls, nearly 400,000 administrative calls, and over 1.6 million radio transmissions annually. We dispatch for 66 Police, Fire, and EMS agencies in three different counties. We also handle landline and VoIP E9-1-1 calls for Aroostook County.
For several years, Penobscot County schools have started implementing silent alarms or tip lines. Each school district expects our PSAP to monitor these tip lines and alarms, but they all use different vendors. As you can imagine, this creates a complicated situation for our staff who already have to manage six different computer screens to execute their daily functions. With over 100 schools in our coverage area and RSUs crossing county lines, this could create a catastrophic problem.
In Maine, we currently have the option to call or text 9-1-1. I firmly believe that utilizing a silent alarm could cause a significant demand in services both in response and training. The more tasks we continue to put on our Emergency Communications Specialists, the more people we need to hire. There is a considerable cost element, not only in the equipment at the schools, but in the Public Safety Answering Points as well.
If the committee would like to move this bill forward, I would suggest a stakeholder group with heavy involvement from Public Safety, specifically Public Safety Answering Points and Emergency Services Communication Bureau staff. A project of this magnitude will fail unless a methodical approach is taken to ensure success at the equipment level and to handle multi-jurisdictional concerns.

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs
Committee, good morning. I am Rep. David Sinclair, proudly representing the people of the City
of Bath, House District 50. I appreciate the opportunity to present LD 168, An Act to Improve
Safety in Public Schools by Requiring Silent Electronic Notification Systems in Classrooms.

While campaigning last fall, I was asked by a constituent when Maine would implement "Alyssa's Law," which I had to admit never having heard of. I promised her I would learn more
about it, and what I learned lead to my filing of this bill.

"Alyssa's Law" is named after a young student, Alyssa Alhadeff, who, at age 14, was a victim of
the 2018 shooting at Marjorie Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. The legislation, being adopted on a state-by-state basis, is intended to improve and accelerate law
enforcement response times during emergencies at public schools, primarily through teacher-
worn silent pushbutton alarms that directly notify local law enforcement agencies.

Thus far, versions of this legislation have been implemented in Florida, New Jersey, New York,
Texas, T6I1l'l6SS6, Utah, and Oklahoma, and implementations are in progress in Connecticut, Pemisylvania, Georgia, Arkansas, Illinois, Kentucky, Michigan, and Mississippi -- the system is a
good idea, and one I hope we can bring to fruition here in Maine as well.

I learned this morning that there is a very similar bill, LD 808, filed by Rep. Mastraccio, to be
heard before this Committee -- I may have filed first, but Anne-Marie filed better, as her bill also
includes important provisions related to training and stipulations regarding security data
protections. I hope to return to testify in favor of LD 808 once that bill is set for hearing, and
hope that at least one of these bills will receive strong Committee support.

District 50: Bath

Thank you for your time and consideration - I am happy to answer any questions committee members may have.
Respectfully,

VICE PRESIDENT RHONDA SPERREY

Ensuring the safety of every single student and staff member is the number one priority for our school leaders. Towards that goal, Maine districts have invested in many new safety initiatives, from building enhancements and notification systems to "badges" that staff can press to call for help.
We also work closely with local law enforcement to ensure appropriate procedures are in place to quickly respond to an emergency, protect our students and quickly notify families. Schools have detailed emergency protocols which are regularly updated through community collaboration. We support the use of any new technologies to complement these efforts and increase communication.
However, our association has two primary concerns regarding the policy proposed in this bill. First, the legislation would seem to require every school to implement a very specific type of silent alert system. We have concerns about a law requiring such a narrowly defined solution, which could limit our local districts' flexibility in choosing and purchasing a system that best meets the unique needs of their communities.

EILEEN E. KING EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR

We also worry about the cost. Some estimates place the cost of implementing this system at upwards of $8,000 per school, adding substantial expenses that are not covered through state assistance.

This bill also requires that, in addition to notifying school personnel and law enforcement, the system "must automatically notify parents of students who subscribe to be notified" when it is activated. Communication with families during an emergency is of utmost importance to our schools, but we worry that this type of automatic notification could result in families overwhelming our phone lines or rushing to school buildings during the initial, critical moments when school personnel and law enforcement are responding to an emergency. This could potentially impede the work of our staff and law enforcement partners in protecting our children.
Again, our school leaders support any tools to better protect our students, and many districts have already purchased their own notification systems towards that goal. Thank you for your time.

Maine E911 Advisory Council
MEMORANDUM
TO:Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Educationand Cultural Affairs
FROM:Maine E911 Advisory Council
DATE:March 11, 2025
SUBJECT:Opposition to LD 168, An Act to Improve Safetyin Public Schools by Requiring Silent Electronic Notification Systems in Classrooms
The Maine E911 Advisory Council writes to express our strong opposition to LD 168, "An Act to Improve Safety in Public Schools by Requiring Silent Electronic Notification Systems in Classrooms." While we understand and share the goal of enhancing safety in our schools, we believe LD 168 is not the most effective or efficient way to achieve this goal and could potentially create unintended negative consequences.
Our concerns are based on several key points:
 Duplication of Existing Systems:Many schools alreadyhave established emergency communication protocols and systems in place, including direct lines to 911, public address systems, and internal communication networks. LD 168 risks duplicating these systems and potentially creating confusion or delays during emergencies.
 Potential for False Alarms:Silent electronic notificationsystems could be prone to accidental activation or misuse, leading to false alarms that divert resources and create unnecessary panic.
 Automatic Notification of Parents:LD 168 mandatesautomatic parent notification for subscribed parents. This notification would likely be a basic emergency alert, lacking any substantive details or instructions. For example, this automatic alert would likely look the same for a fire alarm

activation as it would for an active shooter, or even an accidental activation of a panic button. This eliminates the possibility of a coordinated message from school administrators and public safety personnel to parents. Such messages should provide critical information and instructions, allowing parents to make informed decisions guided by officials. Instead, the automatic notification forces parents to act independently, potentially interfering with public safety response efforts.  First Responder Work Load:The influx of concernedparents at schools during emergencies has been shown to impede first responders and complicate emergency response efforts. Additionally, the anticipated surge in 911 calls following emergency notifications could overwhelm PSAPs, hindering their ability to manage the emergency and obtain crucial information from those directly involved.  Technical and Logistical Challenges:Implementingand maintaining a statewide system of silent electronic notification systems would present significant technical and logistical challenges, including costs for equipment, installation, training, and ongoing maintenance.  Integration with Existing 911 Infrastructure:LD 168does not adequately address how these systems would integrate with the existing 911 infrastructure. There is a high risk that these systems would not provide the necessary information to dispatchers or would create additional work for dispatchers who are already handling emergency calls.  Training and Protocol Issues:Ensuring consistenttraining and protocols across all schools in the state would be a major undertaking. Without proper training and protocols, the systems could be ineffective or even detrimental in an emergency.
We believe that existing emergency communication systems, when properly maintained and utilized, are sufficient to ensure the safety of students and staff in our schools. We urge the committee to consider alternative approaches that would address school safety concerns more effectively and efficiently. These alternatives could include:
 Enhancing training for school staff on existing emergency procedures  Improving communication and coordination between schools and local first
responders  Investing in upgrades to existing communication systems and infrastructure

We appreciate the opportunity to provide input on this important issue. We are available to discuss our concerns in more detail and to work with the committee to find solutions that truly enhance school safety in Maine.
Sincerely,
Joseph Thornton, ENP Maine E911 Advisory Council Chairman

Neither For Nor Against

March 13, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Education and Cultural Affairs (Committee), my name is Maria Jacques, testifying neither for nor against LD 168, An Act to Improve Safety in Public Schools by Requiring Silent Electronic
Notification Systems in Classrooms on behalf of the Public Utilities Commission, Emergency Services Communication Bureau (ESCB).
The ESCB is responsible for implementing and managing Maine's E 9-1 -1 system, which includes
9-1-l call answering equipment, training and 9-1-1 services for all 25 Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs) in the state. In 2024, there were 585,363 9-1-1 calls processed by our PSAPs.
In Maine, 9-1-1 is available from traditional wireline phones, cell phones, and VoIP phones.
Regardless of the type of service, important location information is delivered along with the voice call.
All PSAP personnel are trained on how to process a silent call--an open line where no one speaks-which sometimes happens when a caller is in danger.
Text to 911 is also available. It is designed as an alternative to a traditional call when an individual is hearing impaired or when an individual cannot make a voice call, for example during a home invasion
or a medical emergency that renders an individual incapable of speech.
The primary responsibility of a PSAP is to answer all 911 calls in its local coverage area. Each Maine community is matched with a PSAP. Some PSAPs answer calls for just a couple of communities while others answer calls for over 100. In most cases, PSAP coverage areas do not align with school administrative districts. Over the last few years, PSAPs have struggled to maintain staffing levels and if more tasks are added, additional staff may be needed.
L.D. 168 requires a public elementaiy school or public secondaiy school that enrolls 12 or more students to equip each classroom with a silent electronic notification system. The silent electronic notification system must automatically notify the 9-1-1 system, school security personnel and local law enforcement agencies when manually activated. The system must also automatically notify parents of
students who subscribe to be notified.

LOCATION: 26 Katliciine Drive, Hallowell, ME 04347
PHONE: (207) 287-3831 (VOICE)

MAIL: 18 State House Station, Augusta, ME 04333-0018

TFY users call Maine Relay 71 l

FAX: (207)287-1039

The ESCB has the following concems with the bill as proposed:
1. There are many different silent electronic notification systems on the market. The only ones
that could integrate or automatically notify the 9-1-l system are ones that generate a voice call
or text message. We are currently unaware if this type of system is readily available, and if it is
available, we are unsure if there would be cost implications to integrate this into the 9-1-1
system.
2. If the intent of LD 168 is to provide an over-the-top service (a service that goes into the PSAP
but does not display on the 911 equipment itself), the boundaries of schools do not align with
the boundaries of PSAPs so a PSAP could have several different software programs to purchase, install and monitor. Again, we have concerns about the cost implication this service may have on PSAPs. Ideally, all schools should be required to use the same program or at least utilize a common platform at the PSAPs.
3. False alarms often plague these systems. For PSAPs managing many towns (or schools), this could quickly become overwhelming.
4. While we understand the need to provide information to parents, requiring the notification of
parent of an activation could cause massive panic, hinder the public safety response, and
completely overwhelm the PSAP with inbound calls.
The ESCB is willing to engage in further conversations with the sponsor and stakeholders in order to achieve the goals of this legislation (as Well as LD 808) in a manner that minimizes the costs and complications associated with the implementation of LD 168.
I would be happy to answer any questions or provide additional information for the work session.

TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO
L.D. 168
AN ACT TO IMPROVE SAFETY IN PUBLIC SCHOOLS BY REQUIRING SILENT ELECTRONIC NOTIFICATION SYSTEMS IN CLASSROOMS
March 13, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee. I am Steven Bailey, the executive director for the Maine School Boards Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committee of the Maine School Boards Association in opposition to L.D. 168.
While our association believes deeply in ensuring every student feels safe at school, we are opposed to this bill because we believe it would increase costs to local taxpayers and mandate implementation of a very specific notification program in every classroom across our state. We feel that local schools should have control in crafting systems that best protect their students.
Several tragedies in recent years have highlighted the unfortunate reality of gun violence in our schools. In Maine, every district takes this risk immensely seriously, and student safety is always our top priority. Many schools have added resource officers to serve as liaisons with local police departments, offering protection, safety and swift communication. Our administrators also frequently meet with law enforcement to update their safety and emergency protocols, ensuring that staff and students are wellprotected.
While we encourage and welcome new approaches to enhance security, our association does not view this bill as a wise policy to implement in every Maine classroom. L.D. 168 would mandate a "silent electronic notification system" that would automatically notify 9-1-1, school security, local law enforcement and parents when manually activated in the event of a life-threatening or emergency situation. This bill appears to refer to a very narrow subset of notification systems that a district could purchase, providing our boards and administrators limited flexibility to choose the one that would work best for the needs of their school and community.
Moreover, we are deeply concerned at the substantial costs of this bill. While some Maine schools have already implemented silent notification systems, others have found the costs to be prohibitively expensive - estimated to be in the range of tens of thousands of dollars per district. We view this as an unfunded mandate that would fall on our local taxpayers, who we know cannot afford them.
We want our students and staff to be safe, but our policies should be crafted in a realistic, thought-out way that considers the needs and resources of our schools and communities. For these reasons, we urge you to oppose L.D. 168. Thank you.
